v: Babu neee Maaassu… Mind Blocku!!! Mahesh’s mass comeback is a treat for fans, but for neutral viewers the silly train comedy and weak climax keep it only a time-pass average entertainer.
e: Sarileru Neekevvaru finally lets Mahesh Babu step away from his recent message-heavy films and enjoy a full mass avatar. His comedy timing, punch dialogues and screen presence are refreshing, but an overdone train episode, thin content and a weak, illogical climax make the overall experience much more mixed for a neutral audience.
body:
Babu neee Maaassu… Bomma Mind Blocku!!!!!

For Mahesh Babu fans, Sarileru Neekevvaru is almost what Gabbar Singh was for Pawan Kalyan fans — they are going to enjoy this mass avatar of MB to the core.

For a neutral audience, though, it is more of a time-pass average movie.

I had honestly become a little tired of Mahesh’s seemingly endless run of message-oriented and family films over the previous few years, especially with the similar performance style and sloooww dialogue modulation.

So this movie felt like fresh air simply because it finally explores his mass-entertainer potential again.

And Mahesh completely owns that space.

His trademark comedy timing works, the punchy dialogues suit him, and his dance and grace in the Mind Block song are going to be a proper treat for fans.

Content-wise, there is nothing particularly new here. It follows the familiar mass-film template, but because Mahesh returns to this genre after such a looooong gap, even familiar material feels a little refreshing.

Director Anil Ravipudi seems determined to live up to expectations around his comedy track, and unfortunately that makes him overdo it.

The entire train episode is packed with exaggerated performances from Sangeetha, Rashmika and others.

A certain section of the audience may get irritated with that never-ending silliness — I certainly did 😄 — while people who love this kind of masssss comedy may enjoy it completely.

My daughter was laughing out loud through that whole sequence while I was sitting there wondering when it would finally end, so that probably explains the divide perfectly.

The climax tries to be different, but it is very weak and illogical even by mass-movie standards.

On the positive side, the confrontation scenes involving Prakash Raj, Vijayashanti and Mahesh in the second half are handled superbly, mixing powerful punches with comedy nicely.

DSP’s music is quite ordinary, though the songs are shot well. The BGM is much better and gives the hero-elevation moments exactly the lift they need.

Overall, this feels designed to be a runaway entertainer in B and C centres, where the complete mass package will probably work extremely well.

For audiences expecting stronger content, subtler comedy or a sensible climax, the experience is likely to stay much closer to average.

v: Not for the regular moviegoer, but absolutely a MUST WATCH. Meghna Gulzar keeps the pain, dignity and message simple and effective instead of turning an acid-attack survivor’s story into melodrama.
e: Chhapaak worked for me because Meghna Gulzar treats an extremely painful subject with restraint. The film explores not just an acid-attack survivor’s struggle but also family support, women’s empowerment and the exhausting reality of sustaining a social cause, with Deepika Padukone and Vikrant Massey carrying the emotions without unnecessary drama.
body:
Not for the regular moviegoer… but a MUST WATCH!!!

Meghna Gulzar brilliantly shows the struggles faced by an acid-attack survivor and her family without reducing the subject to one-note suffering.

The film also brings in women’s empowerment and the constant practical struggle involved in running — and financially sustaining — a social cause.

There were a few things I especially loved.

The relationship between the lawyer and her husband is handled beautifully.

There are no giant dialogues or dramatic declarations around his support, yet the film quietly shows how a husband can help his wife chase her dreams by simply getting involved in the basic, everyday things that make those dreams possible 🙏

I also liked the sweet relationship between Amol and Malti.

Personally, I would probably have preferred them to remain friends rather than moving towards romance, but since the film draws from a real-life story, there is not much to argue about there 😄

The lyrics are excellent and the music stays simple, allowing us to feel the pain of acid-attack victims without forcing emotion through loud filmmaking.

The dialogues follow the same approach — simple, effective and never overloaded with drama, yet they still communicate the pain and the message clearly.

Performance-wise, Deepika Padukone has already proved herself many times, so I would not say the acting challenge itself is the surprising part here.

What deserves appreciation is her decision to take up a film like this, because her presence allows the subject to reach a much wider audience.

Vikrant Massey also does a very good job as Amol, particularly in showing the emotions of someone who is deeply committed to a cause but is constantly struggling with the reality of being able to afford that commitment.

Chhapaak is not an easy entertainment watch, and it is not trying to be one.

But for the subject it takes on, and the restraint with which it communicates that subject, it is absolutely worth watching.

v: Rajini’s style plus Anirudh’s BGM can still touch the sky — unfortunately Darbar’s positives pretty much end there. Outdated writing and baffling logic waste the Superstar’s screen presence.
e: Darbar gives Rajinikanth plenty of chances to remind us why his style remains unmatched, and Anirudh’s BGM amplifies those moments wonderfully. But the writing feels badly dated, the logic is often baffling and Murugadoss never builds enough around that star power, leaving only scattered fan moments in an otherwise disappointing film.
body:
Many actors have tried to imitate his style and grace, and Rajinikanth himself has done these gestures a zillion times — yet somehow it is still a treat to watch Thalaivaa’s STYLE!!!

Darbar once again proves that he is the one and only STYLE ICON.

And when Rajini’s style meets Anirudh’s BGM, only the sky is the limit!!!!!

Unfortunately, Darbar’s positives more or less end there.

Was this really written and directed by A.R. Murugadoss?

Man, how could he make a movie filled with material that feels this outdated 😦

I already felt he had lost some form after Spyder — even though I personally liked that film for its different concept — but Darbar made that concern much stronger.

Some of the writing and logic are genuinely baffling.

There is even a scene where the backstory says a father was killed roughly twenty-seven years earlier, while in the present a four- or five-year-old child is shown kissing his photograph and saying, “Miss you, Dad.”

How does that timeline even work? 🙏

Beyond Rajini’s presence and the BGM, there is honestly not much else I felt strongly about.

Anirudh’s background score is excellent, but the songs are almost equally disappointing.

Fans who simply want to enjoy Rajini’s style may find a few portions worth cheering for.

Fans expecting a strong Murugadoss film, though, are probably better off staying away.

The frustrating part is that Rajini still has enormous screen presence, yet the current lot of filmmakers rarely seem to use it fully enough to create the kind of impact we saw in films like Narasimha.

That wasted potential is what makes Darbar more disappointing than merely routine.

v: A routine family-values drama that often feels like Shatamanam Bhavati revisited — but Rao Ramesh almost single-handedly turns hero, villain and comedian and keeps the film alive.
e: Prathi Roju Pandage feels extremely familiar in both story and treatment, with Maruthi’s humour and Raashi Khanna’s TikTok-obsessed character providing most of the variation. The real reason to watch is Rao Ramesh, who carries the routine family drama so completely that Sai Dharam Tej can sometimes feel like he is appearing in an extended cameo.
body:
Story-wise, Prathi Roju Pandage almost felt like a sequel to Shatamanam Bhavati, and even much of the treatment reminded me of the same film.

Director Maruthi adds his trademark humour and gives the heroine the gimmick of being a TikTok addict, but apart from those touches there is very little here that feels different from the many recent so-called family-values movies.

The one person who completely lifts this otherwise routine family drama is Rao Ramesh.

He carries the film on his shoulders so comfortably that after a few scenes you genuinely start feeling that he — and only he — is the HERO, VILLAIN and COMEDIAN of the movie!!!!!

Raashi Khanna does a good job as the TikTok queen, while the rest of the family characters support Rao Ramesh’s terrific performance well.

Sai Dharam Tej, surprisingly, almost feels like he has an extended-cameo kind of role in comparison.

He does a decent job with what he is given, but the movie never really feels like it belongs to him.

There is not much to say about the remaining departments because none of them are particularly bad, but none of them stand out as exceptional either.

Overall, it is a familiar and fairly average family entertainer whose biggest strength is one performer making routine material much more watchable than it might otherwise have been.
